LEARNING PATH LESSON · FEELINGS & KINDNESS · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Share the Space, Work Together, Take Turns & Cheer Others — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson runs the full playdate: four words that handle the crowd — sharing the floor, building together, queuing for the good parts and cheering whoever wins the moment.

What is this?

Share the space, work together, take turns and cheer others are the four playdate words: room for two at the table, many hands on the build, my-go-your-go for the good parts and the cheer that points at someone else.

What does it mean?

Cheering others is the advanced course: a four-year-old who claps for a friend’s success has learned the opposite of jealousy — the feeling that quietly decides how good group life will be for everyone including the cheerer.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ideas: sharing SPACE is easier and different from sharing things (room at the table, room in the game); taking turns means the wait has an END (my-go-your-go, then it rolls back); and cheering is a skill — specific beats generic ("you stacked the BIG one!" outcheers "yay").

Why this matters

This card is the group-practice run for everything the class has taught: feelings named, pause learned, kindness chosen — here it all meets other children, where the weather is real.

What it teaches

Cooperative and turn-based play, spatial generosity, waiting with an end in sight, and other-praising — the celebration of someone else’s success, which research keeps linking to lasting friendships.

Words to learn

share the spacework togethertake turnscheer othersmy goyour goyay

Say this to your child

“"Playdates run on four words. Share the space — the rug, the table, the game: there is room for both of us, scoot in. Work together — many hands build faster: you hold it, I stack it, we both cheer the tower. Take turns — the good parts are worth waiting for, and the wait has an end: my go, your go, my go again. And cheer others — when someone else does something great, YOUR thumbs go up: you stacked the BIG one! Here is the secret about cheering: it feels even better than being cheered. That is not a joke — try it and see."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four words that run a playdate."
  2. Read the panels: two children SHARE THE SPACE over one book, two more WORK TOGETHER with a high-five, the waiting boy TAKEs TURNS, the thumbs-up girl CHEERs OTHERS.
  3. Name the difference: sharing things (the truck) versus sharing SPACE (the rug, the table, the game) — space is easier to start with.
  4. Run the one-block-each build below — all four words in one game.
  5. Close with the cheer practice: everyone invents one specific cheer for someone else’s real success today, and delivers it.

Look closer at the picture

On this card four panels run the playdate: Share the Space, a boy and a girl reading one book together; Work Together, two children high-fiving; Take Turns, a patient boy waiting with a hand on his cheek; and Cheer Others, a girl with both thumbs up — group life drawn at carpet-time scale.

Ask your child

"What is the difference between sharing a toy and sharing the space?" "Does the turn come back?" "What makes a cheer GREAT — yay, or you stacked the big one?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "There is room for both of us!" "My go — then your go!" or the advanced one: "GOOD STACKING, Mia!"

Out in the real world

Playdate mechanics repeat weekly: the crowded craft table (share the space), the bakery-shop game (work together), the single swing (take turns), the sibling’s first pedal strokes (cheer others). Each is a live rep — narrate the word as it happens and the mechanics become manners.

Try it together

One-Block-Each Tower: build a block tower where the ONLY rule is one block each, then pass — no exceptions, grown-ups included. Every placement earns a specific cheer from the previous builder ("tall one! perfect corner!"). The tower falls eventually (they always do) — rebuild rule stands, and so does the cheering. Five minutes, all four words, one laughing family.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we share besides toys? What do we say while waiting? Who is the cheer for?" The space, my-go-your-go, someone else — three answers and the playdate runs itself.

Parent tips

Cheering needs models more than instructions — a household that says "your brother zipped it himself — tell him what you noticed!" raises children who look for material to cheer. And keep turns SHORT at four: the wait is the exercise, so make the reps frequent and tiny; long turns teach only endurance.

This lesson pairs with the Share the Space, Work Together, Take Turns & Cheer Others flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Feelings & Kindness (Class 38).
